This manuscript addresses the problem of learning sequences of events with variable durations. This is an important problem. The revised manuscript was reviewed by two new reviewers and one previous reviewer. The consensus was that the manuscript will be suitable for publication after the following two points are addressed:

1) Time constants of inhibitory neurons:

The choice of synaptic time constants (80ms for exc. and 10ms for inhibition) is very odd. There is no justification provided for these values.

The solution that was proposed by the reviewers is that to solve this issue by redifining the time scale by, say division by 5. So that what now is 80 milliseconds becomes 16 milliseconds. This has to be done consistently throughout the paper, but new simulations are not absolutely necessary. The point can be addressed by careful re-definition of time scales throughout the manuscript, if this is what the authors prefer.

2) The emergence of CNA and fine tuning of the model:

Another crucial parameter is the connections from timer-->messenger and inhibitory neurons--> messenger neurons. These have to be tuned such that messengers only fire when inhibition has gone down. These synapses do not appear to have been learned using the TTL in this model. This point can be addressed by testing robustness with respect to changes in the synaptic weights: what happens if connection weights are change by +/- 29 percent. New simulations are necessary here.

Reviewer 1:

One of the main points raised in the previous review was that of the fine tuning of the parameters. In this revision authors have not done much to address that concern (see below for my comments on their reply). So for now, I maintain that the model is contrived and rests on very strong assumptions for which there is little experimental evidence.

1) The issue of rewards:

Authors write: We have assumed that on every transition between external stimuli, a “novelty” signal causes a global release of a neuromodulator, which acts as a reinforcement signal (see Materials and methods).

This is a big assumption. Clearly, we don’t just make sequences of novel events. Familiar events are also added in sequences with novel events.

2) Time constants of inhibitory neurons:

The choice of synaptic time constants (80ms for exc. and 10ms for inh) is very odd as also noted by the second reviewer - but this is also crucial to the model. But there is no justification provided for these values.

3) The emergence of CNA and fine tuning of the model:

Another crucial parameter is the connections from timer-->messenger and inh neurons--> messenger neurons. These have to be tuned such that messenger only fire when inhibition has gone down - I do not think these synapses have been learned using the TTL in this model.

Authors argue that these synaptic weights can be learned as they have shown in Huerta et al. But CNA architecture is different from the model studied in Huerta et al. Three types of cells in Huerta et al., are all excitatory and there is a global inhibitory population. But for the CNA here we need two excitatory populations and one inhibitory. Moreover, the third inhibitory population cannot serve the function of global inhibition that may give rise to the timer/messenger cells (e.g. following Huerta et al.,). Furthermore, in the Huerta paper number of messenger cells are way too low but here authors have assumed that there are equal number of timer and messenger cells. Therefore, authors’ claim that they have provided a putative mechanism for the emergence of the CNA structure is not correct.

Since authors argue that "there are a number of degenerate sets of parameters" they should show some of those. In addition, since the choice of synaptic time constants is so odd, they should show that the model works when exc. synaptic time constant is smaller than inh time constant - or how close these two time constants can be. When a model has so many parameters it is important to question the robustness of the model.

Authors have shown the robustness of the learning algorithm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) but there are other parameters in the model that are not associated with plastic synapses. How crucial are they? At the outset it is obvious that the synaptic time constant are crucial and for some reason exc. syn time constant has to be longer than inhibitory time constant. Similarly, the connectivity from timer-->messenger and inh-neurons-->messenger needs to be tuned very carefully.

4) The issue of other inhibitory neurons:

My question was not about the detectability. My concern is that besides the inh neurons in the CNA there will be other inhibitory neurons in the network e.g. those needed for the emergence of time/messenger populations. Would their activity cause problems?

5) Biological realism:

I agree with the authors that they have a local learning rule and the rule is biologically plausible. My concern was about using reservoir network (which is fine) and still calling the model (Figure 5) biologically realistic. I also do not understand the use of the term “reservoir”. To me it seems like an attractor network. As the authors know, in reservoir computing we need to train the readout of the “reservoir” to get a specific pattern in response to an input.Reviewer 4:

The paper addresses the problem of learning sequences composed of events of variable duration. This is an important problem and solution using messenger and timer cells is interesting and novel. I am less convinced of the utility of relying on reservoir computing to solve non-Markovian sequences. I wonder whether this can be done using connections between different CAN.

It is not clear whether the primary visual cortex (or a primary sensory area) is the best brain area to draw parallels with the proposed framework. Perhaps hippocampus would be more appropriate. In any case, layer 4 and 5 of primary sensory areas have very different properties and assigning them the same properties detracts from biological plausibility. There is some sequence learning in the visual cortex, but this is not the main effect in primary sensory processing.

claims.source: Although the parts of the model's construction are based upon recent experimental observations in visual cortex (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Cooke et al., 2015), utilizing observed cell types (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013) and laminar structure (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014; Binzegger et al., 2009), many of its key aspects (modularity, heterogenous representations) are illustrative of general principles of sequence learning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The ability of the network to internally learn and recall both duration and order differs from most historical and contemporary models of sequence learning.
claims.source: The ability of the network to internally learn and recall both duration and order, along with its use of a local learning rule that bypasses the need for constant and explicit targets, differs from most historical and contemporary models of sequence learning (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018; Jun and Jin, 2007; Liu and Buonomano, 2009; Maes et al., 2020; Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019; Rajan et al., 2016; DePasquale et al., 2018; Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Nicola and Clopath, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited models.

claims.claim: Chain structure models of neural sequence learning operate in a method akin to synfire chains.
claims.source: Chain structure models of neural sequence learning operate in a method akin to synfire chains (Abeles, 1991) – that is, representations of different individual stimuli are linked together, in order, via feed-forward synaptic connections (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018; Jun and Jin, 2007; Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant models.

claims.claim: Chain-like structures can readily encode order but do not internally encode start times, stop times, or durations of individual elements.
claims.source: While such a chain-like structure can readily encode order, there is nothing internally encoding start times, stop times, or durations of the individual elements of the sequence.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of chain-like models.

claims.claim: Some chain models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock' upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output.
claims.source: Some models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock', upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output, but the fragility of the chain itself can make such output representations very sensitive to noise (Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific model.

claims.claim: The fragility of activity chains can make output representations very sensitive to noise.
claims.source: Some models use the resulting activity chain as a temporal basis or 'clock', upon which elements and their durations can be learned at the level of the output, but the fragility of the chain itself can make such output representations very sensitive to noise (Liu and Buonomano, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific model.

claims.claim: RNNs learn complex sequences by leveraging rich, dynamical representations to approximate target outputs.
claims.source: Unlike explicit feed-forward chain models, RNNs learn complex sequences by leveraging rich, dynamical representations to approximate target outputs.
claims.evidence: This is a general characterization of RNN models based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: RNNs are fully capable of encoding duration and order.
claims.source: RNNs are fully capable of encoding duration and order, and can embed multiple sequences at once.
claims.evidence: This is a general characterization of RNN capabilities based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Common learning rules for RNNs, such as backpropagation through time or FORCE, are biologically unrealistic.
claims.source: However, common learning rules for these models, such as backpropagation through time (BPTT) or FORCE, are biologically unrealistic, as they require some combination of non-local information, precise and symmetrical feedback structures, and/or explicit feedback about the targets at every time point (Whittington and Bogacz, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation and established knowledge about biological plausibility.

claims.claim: Networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent work has shown that networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation (Lillicrap et al., 2016), but this random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales (Murray, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claims.claim: Random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent work has shown that networks can under some conditions learn inputs via random feedback connections rather than backpropagation (Lillicrap et al., 2016), but this random feedback is less effective than BPTT for learning sequences with long time scales (Murray, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claims.claim: The expression of sequences in the brain often follows a compressed encoding, in which order is represented but duration is not.
claims.source: Experimentally, the expression of sequences in the brain often follows a compressed encoding, in which order is represented but duration is not, and sequences are replayed with a time scale dictated by the intrinsic time scales of the circuit (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Davidson et al., 2009; Ji and Wilson, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: There are many cases where neural sequences are learned and replayed at or near their behavioral time scale.
claims.source: However, there are also many cases where neural sequences are learned and replayed at or near their behavioral time scale (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Eichenlaub et al., 2020; Dave and Margoliash, 2000), for which a simple ordered chain is insufficient.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The model's chain-like, modular structure enables it to learn the order of elements.
claims.source: Our model's chain-like, modular structure enables it learn the order of elements, while the recurrent structure within that chain allows it to internally and flexibly learn those elements' duration.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claims.claim: The recurrent structure within the chain allows the model to internally and flexibly learn elements' duration.
claims.source: Our model's chain-like, modular structure enables it learn the order of elements, while the recurrent structure within that chain allows it to internally and flexibly learn those elements' duration.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claims.claim: The structure of the network allows the use of a local, biophysically realistic learning rule to adjust the synaptic weights.
claims.source: The structure of our network allows us to use a local, biophysically realistic learning rule to adjust the synaptic weights.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claims.claim: A transient sequential input is presented during training.
claims.source: A transient sequential input is presented during training, and over the course of training, our learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
claims.evidence: This describes the training procedure used in the model.

claims.claim: Over the course of training, the learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
claims.source: A transient sequential input is presented during training, and over the course of training, our learning rule causes the weights to reach fixed points.
claims.evidence: This describes the behavior of the learning rule during training, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: After training, the network can recall the uncompressed transient activity of the sequential input upon only partial reactivation.
claims.source: After training, the network can then recall the uncompressed transient activity of the sequential input, complete with both duration and order, upon only partial reactivation (e.g. stimulating only the first element in the sequence).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: In a traditional 'chain-like' network with Hebbian learning, order of presented stimuli can be readily encoded by learning directional feed-forward connections between populations.
claims.source: In a traditional 'chain-like' network with Hebbian learning, order of presented stimuli can be readily encoded by learning directional feed-forward connections between populations.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about chain-like networks based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: A simple chain architecture is insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times.
claims.source: However, this simple architecture proves insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times, as intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through the network (Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through a chain network.
claims.source: However, this simple architecture proves insufficient for internally representing the duration of presented stimuli and their specific start and end times, as intrinsic time constants determine the speed at which the signal travels through the network (Murray and Escola, 2017; Martinez et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The network of spiking neurons can learn the order, duration, and specific timing of sequence elements.
claims.source: In this work we present a network of spiking neurons that can learn the order, duration, and specific timing of sequence elements.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the Results section, particularly in Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: The model uses local and biophysically realistic learning rules, in contrast to most RNN models.
claims.source: This model uses local and biophysically realistic learning rules, in contrast to most RNN models (DePasquale et al., 2018; Laje and Buonomano, 2013; Sussillo and Abbott, 2009; Nicola and Clopath, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited RNN models.

claims.claim: In the model, order is learned by modifying the feed-forward synaptic efficacies between modules.
claims.source: As in the 'chain-like' models, the order is learned by modifying the feed-forward synaptic efficacies between modules.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The duration of each element is learned via modification of the recurrent connections within each module.
claims.source: Unlike those models, the duration of each element is learned via modification of the recurrent connections within each module (Fiete et al., 2010; Pereira and Brunel, 2019; Klos et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Additional structure within each module and in the allowed connections between modules allows the model to avoid compression during recall while using relatively simple local learning rules.
claims.source: In order to solve this problem, we assume additional structure within each module and in the allowed connections between modules. This additional structure allows us to avoid compression during recall while using relatively simple local learning rules.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claims.claim: The cellular response types generated by this network are consistent with experimental observation.
claims.source: Consequently, the cellular response types generated by this network are consistent with experimental observation (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015), as described below.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The network is composed of different modules that are selectively activated via feed-forward connections by different external stimuli.
claims.source: Our network is composed of different modules that are selectively activated via feed-forward connections by different external stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: Within each module, there are two populations of excitatory cells as well as inhibitory cells.
claims.source: Within each module, there are two populations of excitatory cells as well as inhibitory cells (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: The excitatory cells in both populations are identical in their intrinsic properties but differ in their learned and fixed connections with other cells.
claims.source: The excitatory cells in both populations are identical in their intrinsic properties but differ in their learned and fixed connections with other cells within the module and in different modules.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claims.claim: Timer cells learn strong recurrent connections with other Timer cells within the module.
claims.source: The 'Timer' cells learn strong recurrent connections with other Timer cells within the module.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Strong recurrent connectivity in Timer cells results in long-lasting transient activity, which is used to represent the duration of a given stimuli.
claims.source: This strong recurrent connectivity results in long-lasting transient activity, which is used to represent the duration of a given stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model represents duration, as shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Previous studies have analyzed in detail the relationship between recurrent connectivity and duration of resulting transient activity following a stimulus.
claims.source: Previous studies have analyzed in detail the relationship between recurrent connectivity and duration of resulting transient activity following a stimulus (Gavornik et al., 2009; Gavornik and Shouval, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Timers excite the inhibitory cells and the Messenger cells.
claims.source: Timers also excite the inhibitory cells and the 'Messenger' cells.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Inhibitory cells have roughly the same temporal profile as Timers but decay slightly more quickly.
claims.source: Since the inhibitory cells receive input from the Timers, they have roughly the same temporal profile. However, inhibitory cells in the module decay slightly more quickly than their Timer counterparts, thanks to a combination of shorter time constants for synaptic activation (80 ms for excitatory, 10 ms for inhibitory), and small Timer to inhibitory weights (there are a number of degenerate sets of parameters which can facilitate quickly decaying inhibitory cells) (Huertas et al., 2015) (see 'Materials and methods' and Supplementary materials for more details).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture and dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Messenger cells selectively fire at the end of the Timers' transient activity.
claims.source: Owing to this temporal offset, Messenger cells selectively fire at the end of the Timers' transient activity, since they receive input from both the Timer cells and the (faster decaying) inhibitory cells.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: The temporally specific profile of the Messenger cells enables them to convey a temporally specific transition between elements.
claims.source: The temporally specific profile of the Messenger cells enables them to convey a temporally specific transition between elements, via learned feed-forward connections to Timer cells in other modules.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model architecture enables specific functions.

claims.claim: The Timer/inhibitory/Messenger modular architecture can be constructed in a number of redundant ways, including simply via random distributions of connections.
claims.source: The Timer/inhibitory/Messenger modular architecture can be constructed in a number of redundant ways, including simply via random distributions of connections (see previous work (Huertas et al., 2015) for a more detailed analysis).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The learning rule is based on two competing, synapse-specific, Hebbian-activated eligibility traces: one for long-term potentiation (LTP) and one for long-term depression (LTD).
claims.source: For learning, we use a previously described reinforcement learning rule based on two competing, synapse-specific, Hebbian-activated eligibility traces (Huertas et al., 2016; He et al., 2015): one for long-term potentiation (LTP) and one for long-term depression (LTD) (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning rule used in the model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The presence of Hebbian activity at a given synapse activates the two traces at different rates and to different saturation levels.
claims.source: The presence of Hebbian activity at a given synapse activates the two traces at different rates (and to different saturation levels), and the absence of Hebbian activity causes the traces to decay at different rates.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning rule dynamics.

claims.claim: The change in synaptic weight is determined by the difference in eligibility traces upon presentation of a reinforcement signal.
claims.source: The change in synaptic weight is determined simply by the difference in these traces upon presentation of a reinforcement signal.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning rule, as shown in Equation 14.

claims.claim: On every transition between external stimuli, a 'novelty' signal causes a global release of a neuromodulator, which acts as a reinforcement signal.
claims.source: We have assumed that on every transition between external stimuli, a 'novelty' signal causes a global release of a neuromodulator, which acts as a reinforcement signal (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claims.claim: The assumption of a temporally precise but spatially widespread neuromodulatory signal is consistent with recent recordings in several neuromodulatory systems.
claims.source: The assumption of a temporally precise but spatially widespread neuromodulatory signal might seem at odds with common notions of temporally broad neuromodulator release, but they are indeed consistent with recent recordings in several neruomodulatory systems (Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Hangya et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions.
claims.source: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions (Yagishita et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2017; Brzosko et al., 2017), and eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex (He et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Eligibility traces for LTP have been found in multiple brain regions (Yagishita et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2017; Brzosko et al., 2017), and eligibility traces for both LTP and LTD have been found in both visual and prefrontal cortex (He et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: The eligibility trace learning rule can solve the temporal credit assignment problem.
claims.source: We have used this rule because it can solve the temporal credit assignment problem, allowing the network to associate events distal in time, and because it reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks (Huertas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The eligibility trace learning rule reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks.
claims.source: We have used this rule because it can solve the temporal credit assignment problem, allowing the network to associate events distal in time, and because it reaches fixed points in both recurrent and feed-forward learning tasks (Huertas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: Using the described rule and architecture within a single module, the network naturally generates cells that learn to be active for the duration of the stimulus (Timers) and other cells that activate toward the end of the stimulus duration (Messengers).
claims.source: Using this rule and the described architecture within a single module, we find (Figure 2a) that the network naturally generates cells that learn to be active for the duration of the stimulus (Timers), and other cells that activate toward the end of the stimulus duration (Messengers).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Timer cells learn the duration of the stimulus via changes in the excitatory synaptic efficacies within the Timer population.
claims.source: The Timer cells learn the duration of the stimulus via changes in the excitatory synaptic efficacies within the Timer population.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Messenger cells evolve their specific temporal profile due to the temporal profiles of their fixed excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the Timer cells and the inhibitory cells.
claims.source: The Messenger cells evolve their specific temporal profile due to the temporal profiles of their fixed excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the Timer cells and the inhibitory cells.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: The model results are consistent with experimental observations in V1 circuits that learn the duration between a stimulus and a reward.
claims.source: These results are consistent with experimental observations in V1 circuits that learn the duration between a stimulus and a reward (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013), as shown in Figure 2b.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and comparison to Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The model results replicate previous results using a learning rule with a single trace.
claims.source: These results replicate our previous results (Huertas et al., 2015) which used a learning rule with a single trace (Gavornik et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The modular microcircuit acts as a 'core neural architecture' (CNA), an elemental package of basic temporal neural responses.
claims.source: This modular microcircuit, in which both Timer and Messenger cells emerge from learning, acts as a 'core neural architecture' (CNA) (Huertas et al., 2015), an elemental package of basic temporal neural responses which can then be used within the larger network to create more complicated representations.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The CNA functions as the basic microcircuit for the sequence model.
claims.source: This CNA functions as the basic microcircuit for our sequence model, and each 'element' of an input sequence is represented by one of these CNA circuits.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claims.claim: The individual CNAs are plastic, as their temporal properties are not fixed but adapt to the environment through recurrent learning in the Timer population.
claims.source: One must note that the individual CNAs are plastic, as their temporal properties are not fixed but adapt to the environment, through recurrent learning in the Timer population.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism.

claims.claim: The model places distinct CNAs sensitive to particular visual stimuli in a columnar structure.
claims.source: In a structure akin to the microcircuits found in cortical columns (Potjans and Diesmann, 2014), this model places distinct CNAs sensitive to particular visual stimuli in a columnar structure, as shown in Figure 3a.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3a, supported by citation.

claims.claim: There is soft winner-take-all (WTA) inhibition between the columns to prevent spurious excitation in the noisy, spiking network.
claims.source: To prevent spurious excitation in our noisy, spiking network, there is soft winner-take-all (WTA) inhibition between the columns (see 'Materials and methods' and 'Discussion' for more details).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claims.claim: When presenting a sequence of visual stimuli, different CNAs in turn become activated in sequence.
claims.source: When presenting a sequence of visual stimuli, different CNAs in turn become activated in sequence.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics, as shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Timer cells within CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections.
claims.source: Timer cells within those CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections, while order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
claims.source: Timer cells within those CNAs learn the duration of their particular stimuli via recurrent connections, while order is learned via feed-forward connections from Messengers in one column to Timers in a subsequently presented column.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The modular architecture can overcome the problem of sequence compression encountered by 'chain-like' models.
claims.source: We will show that this modular architecture can overcome the problem of sequence compression encountered by 'chain-like' models.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3e, where the network recalls the sequence without compression.

claims.claim: The network is capable of robustly learning sequences of temporal intervals.
claims.source: Using the above described architecture and learning rule (see 'Materials and methods' for more details), the network is capable of robustly learning sequences of temporal intervals.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3-5.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the network learning a sequence of four different elements, of duration 500, 1000, 700, and 1800 ms.
claims.source: Figure 3 shows the network learning a sequence of four different elements, of duration 500, 1000, 700, and 1800 ms.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The inputs are modeled after lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses to spot stimuli.
claims.source: In this example, the inputs are modeled after lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) responses to spot stimuli (Ruksenas et al., 2007; Mastronarde, 1987, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but more generally one may consider these stimuli to be oriented gratings, specific natural images in a movie, or non-visual stimuli such as pitches of sounds in a song.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model inputs, supported by citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Before learning, presentation of the blue stimulus only produces a transient response in the CNA microcircuit housed in the blue-sensitive column.
claims.source: Before learning, presentation of the blue stimulus only produces a transient response in the CNA microcircuit housed in the blue-sensitive column (Figure 3b).

claims.source: During learning (Figure 3c,d), a sequence of stimuli is presented, and microcircuits in their respective columns learn to represent the duration of the stimulus which activates them.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3c and 3d.

claims.claim: The different microcircuits learn to 'chain' together in the order in which they were stimulated.
claims.source: The different microcircuits also learn to 'chain' together in the order in which they were stimulated.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3c and 3d.

claims.claim: After learning, presentation of the blue stimulus triggers a 'recall' of the entire sequence.

claims.claim: The network is capable of learning sequences of temporal intervals where the individual elements can be anywhere from ~300 to ~1800 ms in duration.
claims.source: The network is capable of learning sequences of temporal intervals where the individual elements can be anywhere from ~300 to ~1800 ms (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2) in duration, which agrees with the observed ranges used for training V1 circuits (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Shuler and Bear, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The network itself shows realistic spiking statistics, with interspike interval coefficients (ISIs) of variation near 1.
claims.source: The network itself shows realistic spiking statistics, with interspike interval coefficients (ISIs) of variation near 1.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The resulting firing rates are roughly consistent with the experimentally observed Timers and Messengers.
claims.source: The resulting firing rates are also roughly consistent with the experimentally observed Timers and Messengers (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison to Figure 2.

claims.claim: In simulations, the network has been able to learn a sequence of up to eight elements.
claims.source: In simulations we have been able to learn a sequence of up to eight elements (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

claims.claim: The upper limit on the number of elements which can be learned in a sequence has not been fully explored due to the computational time required.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claims.claim: Sequences of four elements were chosen to match experimental results.
claims.source: For this work, sequences of four elements were chosen to match experimental results (Gavornik and Bear, 2014).

claims.claim: Similar results are obtained with a low dimensional rate model in which the activity of each population is presented by a single dynamical variable.
claims.source: The model presented here is a high dimensional spiking model, but similar results are obtained with a low dimensional rate model in which the activity of each population is presented by a single dynamical variable (for details, see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).

claims.claim: Before training, presentation of an isolated stimulus only evokes a transient response of the CNA sensitive to that specific stimulus.
claims.source: Before training, presentation of an isolated stimulus only evokes a transient response of the CNA sensitive to that specific stimulus, since the Timer cells have yet to learn any recurrent connections, and the Messenger cells have yet to establish any feed-forward connections to the Timer cells in other columns (Figure 4a).

claims.claim: During training, a particular sequence of inputs is presented and then repeated over many trials.
claims.source: During training, a particular sequence of inputs is presented and then repeated over many trials.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claims.claim: Hebbian activity in the network triggers activation of synapse-specific LTP and LTD associated eligibility traces.
claims.source: Hebbian activity in the network triggers activation of synapse-specific LTP and LTD associated eligibility traces, which are then converted into changes in synaptic connections upon neuromodulator release (purple arrows in Figure 4), occurring here closely after a change in stimuli (see Equations 8, 9, and 14 in 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning mechanism, as shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Each trial pushes the weights in the network toward their fixed points.
claims.source: Each trial pushes the weights in the network toward their fixed points (Equations 17 and 18 in 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning dynamics, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: Hebbian activity within the Timer population causes activation of their respective eligibility traces, and subsequently an increase in their recurrent connections.
claims.source: Hebbian activity within the Timer population causes activation of their respective eligibility traces, and subsequently an increase in their recurrent connections (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: As lateral connections grow, Timer cells sustain their activity for longer, 'extending' their firing profile out in time toward the neuromodulator signal associated with the start of the subsequent stimulus.
claims.source: As these lateral connections grow, Timer cells sustain their activity for longer, 'extending' their firing profile out in time toward the neuromodulator signal associated with the start of the subsequent stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the learning dynamics, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: As Timer cells extend their activity, Messenger cells get 'dragged' along, eventually coactivating with Timer cells of the column which is stimulated next.
claims.source: As this occurs, Messenger cells get 'dragged' along by the Timer cells, eventually coactivating with Timer cells of the column which is stimulated next (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: Hebbian coactivation of Messenger and Timer cells triggers the eligibility traces of feed-forward synaptic connections.
claims.source: This Hebbian coactivation triggers the eligibility traces of these feed-forward synaptic connections, before they too are converted into synaptic weight changes by the neuromodulator 'novelty' signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: After many trials (50–100 for the examples in this paper), weights in the network reach their steady-state values.
claims.source: After many trials (50–100 for the examples in this paper), weights in the network reach their steady-state values (see 'Materials and methods', Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and learning is complete.

results.result: The model consists of a modular, spiking neural network with a microcolumn-based architecture where each module contains Timer and Messenger excitatory cell populations plus inhibitory cells. Timer cells learn strong recurrent connections to represent stimulus duration, while Messenger cells fire at the end of Timer activity to signal transitions between sequence elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C38-C47, C63-C66 describe the core architecture and are directly demonstrated in Figures 2a and 3a. The emergence of Timer and Messenger cell types with appropriate temporal profiles is shown in Figure 2a, and the modular columnar organization is illustrated in Figure 3a. The mathematical formulations in the Materials and methods section provide the mechanistic basis for these dynamics.

results.result: Learning is performed via a biophysically realistic two-trace eligibility learning rule (TTL) where LTP and LTD traces are activated by Hebbian activity at different rates and converted to synaptic weight changes upon neuromodulator release triggered by stimulus transitions. This rule solves the temporal credit assignment problem and reaches fixed points.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 describe the TTL rule, which is mathematically defined in Equations 8-18 and demonstrated to reach fixed points in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2. The biological plausibility is supported by citations to experimental evidence for eligibility traces (C54, C55). The rule's ability to solve temporal credit assignment is demonstrated through successful sequence learning in Figures 3-5.

results.result: Before training, the network contains no memory of sequences and only produces transient responses to individual stimuli. After training on a sequence (e.g., 500, 1000, 700, 1800 ms elements), presentation of only the first element triggers recall of the entire learned sequence without temporal compression.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C75-C78, C86-C97 describe the learning and recall process demonstrated in Figure 3b-e and Figure 4a-c. Before learning (Figure 3b, 4a), only transient responses occur. During learning (Figure 3c-d, 4b), weights evolve toward fixed points as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c. After learning (Figure 3e, 4c), the first stimulus triggers complete sequence recall with correct timing, demonstrating no compression (C97).

results.result: The model's chain-like modular structure enables learning of sequence order via feed-forward connections between Messenger and Timer cells across modules, while recurrent connections within Timer populations enable learning of element duration. Both reach mathematically defined fixed points.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24, C34-C35, C69-C70, C98-C100 describe the dual learning mechanism. Figure 4 demonstrates how feed-forward connections learn order while recurrent connections learn duration. The fixed points are mathematically derived in Equations 17-18 and empirically demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2. This separation of order and duration learning is a key architectural feature enabling the model's capabilities.

results.result: The network can learn sequences with individual elements ranging from ~300 to ~1800 ms in duration, with recalled times generally matching input times to within 10%. The model can learn sequences of up to at least eight elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C107, C177 specify the model's operational range. Figure 3—figure supplement 2 demonstrates the 10% accuracy claim. Figure 3—figure supplement 5 shows successful learning of an 8-element sequence. The duration range (300-1800 ms) is stated to agree with experimental observations in V1 (citations to Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Shuler and Bear, 2006), providing external validation.

results.result: The model exhibits robustness to parameter variations, successfully recalling learned sequences when fixed CNA connections are modified by ±20%, when learning parameters are randomly varied, and when excitatory time constants are reduced from 80 to 20 ms (though shorter time constants limit learnable durations).
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112, C116 describe robustness properties demonstrated in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2. Figure 5 shows successful recall with ±20% variations in fixed connections. Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrates preserved mean reported times with randomized learning parameters. Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows the network functions with 20 ms time constants for 500 ms elements but fails for 1000 ms elements, supporting the limitation claim in C116.

results.result: An extended three-stage model incorporating a fixed recurrent reservoir network and a sparse pattern network can learn and recall non-Markovian sequences with repeated elements (e.g., BGBRBO) where transitions depend on history, not just the current state.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C124, C127-C132, C134-C139, C152-C154, C178 describe the extended model architecture and its capabilities. Figure 6 illustrates the three-stage architecture. Figure 7 demonstrates successful learning and recall of the non-Markovian sequence BGBRBO, where blue transitions to three different elements depending on history. The necessity of all three components (modular network, reservoir, sparse network) is argued in C153-C154 based on their interdependent functions.

results.result: The three-stage model can simultaneously learn two sequences with a shared element (BRO and GRP) and correctly recall each sequence based on the initial stimulus, making appropriate history-dependent transitions from the shared element (red). Recall is robust to perturbations in the reservoir's initial state.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 describe simultaneous learning of multiple non-Markovian sequences. Figure 8a-b demonstrates that stimulation with blue correctly recalls BRO while stimulation with green correctly recalls GRP, with red transitioning appropriately in each case. Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrates robustness to reservoir perturbations. This shows the model can handle multiple overlapping sequences, a more complex non-Markovian scenario.

results.result: Using the TTL rule and CNA architecture, the network naturally generates Timer cells that learn to be active for stimulus duration and Messenger cells that activate toward the end of stimulus duration. These results are consistent with experimental observations in V1 circuits and replicate previous modeling results.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62, C81 describe the emergence of cell types and comparison to experimental data. Figure 2a demonstrates the emergence of Timer and Messenger cells with appropriate temporal profiles. Figure 2b shows schematic experimental data from V1 for comparison. The consistency with experimental observations (C61) is supported by citations to Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; Chubykin et al., 2013. Replication of previous results (C62) is supported by citations to Huertas et al., 2015 and Gavornik et al., 2009.

results.result: The model's ability to internally learn and recall both duration and order using local, biophysically realistic learning rules differs from most historical and contemporary sequence learning models (chain models and RNNs). The modular architecture with heterogeneous cell types implicitly performs credit assignment by decomposing the complex task into simpler subtasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C33, C179-C182, C204, C206, C208, C259 compare the model to existing approaches. The comparison to chain models (C12-C15, C30-C31) and RNNs (C16-C20) is supported by citations and logical arguments about their limitations. The novelty claim (C180) is supported by comparison to cited prior work showing they either lack biological realism, don't learn both duration and order, or are highly parameter-sensitive (C181-C182). The credit assignment argument (C206) is a theoretical interpretation of how the architecture enables local learning.

results.result: The network shows realistic spiking statistics with interspike interval coefficients of variation near 1. Temporal accuracy of recall depends on multiple factors due to network stochasticity, with effects washing out over many trials. The model shows no intrinsic bias toward over- or under-predicting.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C104-C106, C108 describe statistical properties of the spiking network. Figure 3—figure supplement 4 demonstrates ISI coefficients of variation of 1.01 for Timers and 0.75 for Messengers, supporting C80. The discussion of stochastic effects (C104-C106) is supported by the variability shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-b. The lack of systematic bias (C108) is an empirical observation from the simulations.

results.result: Similar results are obtained with a low-dimensional rate-based model where each population is represented by a single dynamical variable. The rate-based approximation produces results similar to the full spiking model.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C161-C164 describe the rate-based approximation. Figure 3—figure supplement 6 directly demonstrates that the rate-based model produces similar results to the spiking model for the Markovian case. This is used to justify the use of rate-based models for the computationally expensive non-Markovian simulations (C161, C163). The similarity provides evidence that the key results are not artifacts of spiking dynamics.

results.result: The model makes several testable predictions: (1) Timer and Messenger cell types will be present during visual sequence learning in V1, (2) distinct populations will be sensitive to distinct stimuli, (3) Messenger cells will more strongly connect to subsequent Timer cells after learning, (4) learning long/short sequences will increase/decrease Timer lateral connections, and (5) inhibitory cells will have Timer-like but faster-decaying profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C203 describe experimental predictions. These are logical consequences of the model architecture and learning dynamics. C197-C199 cite experimental support (Gavornik and Bear, 2014) showing Timer-like responses in layer V and Messenger-like responses in layer II/III, which is consistent with the model's predictions. The other predictions (C200-C203) follow from the model's learning rules and architecture as demonstrated in Figures 2-4, though they await experimental validation.

results.result: The model's construction is based on experimental observations in visual cortex, including observed cell types, laminar structure, and eligibility traces. Various model components and parameter choices are supported by experimental evidence and prior theoretical work.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C21-C22, C37, C43, C48, C53-C55, C113-C115, C191, C193, C222-C223, C227-C229 cite experimental and theoretical support for model components. These claims are supported by extensive citations to experimental studies (e.g., Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Shuler and Bear, 2006; Liu et al., 2015; He et al., 2015; Yagishita et al., 2014) and prior modeling work (e.g., Huertas et al., 2015; Gavornik and Shouval, 2011). The citations provide external validation for the biological plausibility of model assumptions.

results.result: The non-Markovian model has limitations: repeated elements have the same duration due to single attractor per population (C140), sparse patterns show some overlap causing slight activation of incorrect transitions (C148-C150), and parameters were empirically chosen rather than optimized (C151). The implementation uses rate-based dynamics for computational efficiency, though spiking implementations are likely feasible (C165-C168).
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141, C148-C151, C165-C169 acknowledge limitations and implementation choices. C140 correctly identifies that the TTL rule supports only one attractor per population, explaining why repeated elements (blue in BGBRBO) have the same duration in Figure 7d. C148 notes the slight activation of incorrect transitions visible in Figure 8, which is explained by incomplete separation of sparse patterns (C149-C150). The use of rate-based dynamics (C161, C165) is justified by computational efficiency, with speculation about spiking implementations (C166-C168).

results.result: In simulations, the network has learned sequences of up to eight elements. The upper limit has not been fully explored due to computational time. Sequences of four elements were chosen to match experimental results.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 describe practical limitations and design choices. C82 is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 5. C83 honestly acknowledges that the upper limit is unknown due to computational constraints. C84 explains the choice of four-element sequences with citation to experimental work (Gavornik and Bear, 2014), showing the model was designed to match experimental paradigms.

results.result: While the results shown use the two-trace learning (TTL) rule, the network can also be trained with a single-trace learning rule with similar results. TTL was chosen for biological realism, but the novel capabilities primarily result from the network architecture combined with a history-dependent learning rule.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118, C256-C258 discuss alternative learning rules. C118 and C256 state that single-trace rules can replicate results, supported by citations to Gavornik et al., 2009 and Gavornik and Shouval, 2011. C257 speculates that any rule solving temporal credit assignment would work. C258-C259 correctly attribute the model's capabilities primarily to architecture rather than the specific learning rule, which is consistent with the emphasis on modular structure throughout the paper.

results.result: Multiple brain regions can learn temporal sequences (C1). Chain models can encode order but not duration (C12-C15, C29-C31), while RNNs can encode both but use biologically unrealistic learning rules (C16-C20). Markovian models cannot handle sequences with repeated elements followed by different elements (C119-C121). Non-Markovian sequence learning is behaviorally ubiquitous (C122-C123).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C20, C29-C31, C119-C123, C173-C174, C205 provide background knowledge and motivation. These are general statements about the field supported by citations to relevant literature. C1 is supported by citations to experimental studies (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012; etc.). The characterizations of chain models (C12-C15) and RNNs (C16-C20) are supported by citations and represent established knowledge. The Markovian limitation (C119-C121) is a formal property. The ubiquity of non-Markovian learning (C122-C123) is supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2020.

results.result: The model includes soft winner-take-all (WTA) inhibition between columns to prevent spurious excitation in the noisy spiking network. This can be implemented as long-range excitatory connections to local inhibition. Timer cells learn only within-column connections, while Messenger cells learn only to Timer cells outside their column.
results.evaluation: Claims C67, C217-C221, C224 describe architectural constraints. The WTA inhibition (C67, C217) is described as necessary for the spiking network (C219) and is illustrated in Figures 9a-b showing two equivalent implementations (C218). The learning restrictions (C220-C221) are design choices justified by simplifying computation while maintaining functionality (C224). These restrictions are supported by citation to previous work showing all connections are learnable (C222).

results.result: In the three-stage model, the reservoir receives input from the modular network, not the environment. If the modular network doesn't learn, reservoir inputs won't be generated appropriately. During learning, the entire sequence is presented, but for recall, only the first element is needed. This differs from typical reservoir computing where input changes would change output.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C160, C185-C189 explain the interdependence of model components and differences from standard reservoir computing. C155-C156 correctly note that the reservoir depends on the modular network's learned representations. C157-C158 describe the training/recall protocol demonstrated in Figures 7-8. C159-C160 correctly distinguish this from typical reservoir computing. C186 emphasizes the modular network's crucial role. C188 describes the disambiguation requirement for recall. These are logical inferences about the model's operation supported by the architecture and results.

results.result: The viability of the three-stage architecture demonstrates that the columnar network can be used as a building block in more complicated tasks and that even complex tasks like non-Markovian sequence learning don't require non-local learning rules. The model combines highly recurrent networks in a larger architecture to maintain local learning rules.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172, C175 draw conclusions about the three-stage model's implications. C170-C171 are supported by the successful demonstration of non-Markovian learning in Figures 7-8 using only local learning rules. C172 speculates about alternative architectures, which is reasonable given the conceptual nature of the demonstration. C175 summarizes the model's approach of combining recurrent networks with architectural constraints, which is demonstrated throughout the paper.

results.result: Another recently proposed model based on a periodic timing network uses biologically plausible learning rules for non-Markovian sequences but cannot learn arbitrarily long self-terminating sequences or learn and separately replay multiple sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C184 compare to another model (Maes et al., 2020). C183 is supported by citation. C184 claims limitations of that model based on comparison to Figures 7-8, but this comparison may not be entirely fair without detailed analysis of that model's capabilities. The claim that it "cannot" do these things is strong and would require more thorough comparison. However, the authors' model does demonstrate these capabilities, so the comparison serves to highlight their model's strengths.

results.result: The reservoir and sparse network components could arise from projections from other cortical or subcortical areas, or could be part of the same cortical network with functional segregation. The functional modularity could be physically compartmentalized in columns and layers, though this is not strictly required.
results.evaluation: Claims C190, C192, C196 speculate about biological implementation. These are reasonable speculations given the model's functional properties, but they are explicitly presented as possibilities rather than predictions. C191 cites functionally similar networks in dentate gyrus and cerebellum, providing some support, but the specific mapping of model components to brain regions remains speculative. These claims appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about biological implementation.

results.result: Ideally, the network should be able to learn sequences which are in themselves non-Markovian (ABACAD) as well as simultaneous combinations of sequences which are non-Markovian when learned together (ACE and BCD). For the network to learn and recall non-Markovian sequences, it must keep track of its history and use this history to inform transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 describe goals and requirements for non-Markovian learning. C125 states what the network "should" be able to do, presenting ABACAD as an example. However, the demonstrated results (Figures 7-8) show BGBRBO and BRO/GRP, not ABACAD. While the model handles non-Markovian sequences, the specific capability for ABACAD-type sequences is not demonstrated. C126 correctly identifies the logical requirement for history-dependence, which is addressed by the reservoir and sparse network.
